query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of titanium to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will induce the in‐situ formation of stable, nanometer-scale precipitates that promote a protective, self‐lubricating surface layer, thereby maintaining low friction and reducing wear from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix with a single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Alloying with a controlled minor addition of titanium to trigger precipitation of secondary phases.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted under a constant load and ambient atmosphere across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometer-scale Ti-rich precipitates (or associated thermally stable oxide dispersions) that form during processing and/or sliding.
generation.mechanism: The Ti addition is expected to promote the formation of stable precipitates that, at lower temperatures, impede dislocation motion to reduce wear, and at higher temperatures, transform or oxidize to form a continuous, protective, self-lubricating surface layer that mitigates thermally induced increases in friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the Ti-modified variant will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate consistently across the entire temperature range tested.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without any titanium addition.
generation.boundary: The improvement is targeted for sliding contacts under ambient conditions with test temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C and under similar load conditions as those used for baseline studies.
generation.uncertainty: The exact phase evolution, optimal titanium concentration, and balance between precipitate volume fraction and tribological performance remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one set of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and another set of CoCrFeNi alloy with a minor Ti addition (optimized via preliminary studies). Subject both sets to controlled sliding wear tests over a temperature range of room temperature to 800 °C under identical loads and ambient conditions. Use post-test characterization (e.g., SEM, TEM, XRD, and surface chemistry analysis) to confirm precipitate formation and surface oxide characteristics.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss)
Microstructural analysis for precipitate presence and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Ti-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower coefficient of friction and wear rate) over the full temperature range compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy or if the expected stable precipitates/surface layer are not observed.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
